opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think "jagged" is the right word for it, and the first thing I'd say is that the jaggedness is less mysterious than it looks once you think about where the capabilities come from.

These models get good at things in proportion to how much signal they've seen and how verifiable that signal is. Competition math and coding have very clean feedback: the proof checks or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. So when you put a lot of reinforcement learning compute into those domains, you get these spiky, superhuman-looking results. Then you ask the same model to count objects in an image, or keep track of a physical setup over a long conversation, and it stumbles on something a five-year-old would get right. That's not because those tasks are harder in any absolute sense. It's because humans got that stuff for free from evolution and from years of embodied experience, and it's underrepresented in text and hard to write a clean reward for.

So I think part of what we're seeing is that human intuition about "easy" and "hard" is calibrated to human development, not to the structure of the problem. Moravec pointed this out decades ago, and it's still basically true.

The second thing I'd say is that the frontier is jagged, but it's not static. A lot of the things people pointed to a couple of years ago as the obvious gaps, like multi-step reasoning, catching your own mistakes, or knowing when you don't know, have filled in a lot. And the way they filled in is pretty instructive. It usually wasn't a special-purpose fix for that one failure. It came from a more general improvement, like letting the model think longer, or training it to verify its own work. When you lift the general reasoning floor, a lot of the valleys come up at once.

Where I'd be careful is in assuming the remaining valleys will all fill in the same way. Some of them are probably about data and evaluation: we just haven't measured them well or trained on them deliberately. But some might point at something more structural, like how the models handle long-horizon state, continual learning, or grounding in the physical world. Figuring out which valleys are which is honestly one of the more interesting research questions right now.

And practically, for anyone building on these models, the jaggedness is the reason evals matter so much. You can't assume that because a model aced some very hard benchmark it'll be reliable on your simple-looking task. You have to test the specific thing you care about. The models are general, but they're not uniformly general yet.

r001.rationale: The response attributes uneven capabilities to differences in training signal, verifiability, embodied experience, and reward difficulty. It mentions long conversations and long-horizon state, but does not attribute much of the unevenness to limited context.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts models’ development with humans’ evolution and embodied experience, but does not say that humans transfer lessons from one task to future tasks more naturally than current AI models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the jagged frontier is one of the most important things to internalize if you want to have good intuitions about where these models are going. The thing that trips people up is that they want a single scalar for intelligence. They want to say the model is at a high school level, or a PhD level, and then reason from there. And that mental model just breaks immediately, because you'll have a model that can get a gold medal performance on the IMO and then fail to count the number of r's in a word, or get confused by a slightly rephrased riddle that a ten-year-old would get.

The way I think about it is that human intuition about what's hard is calibrated on humans. We find certain things trivial because evolution spent a very long time optimizing us for them. Spatial reasoning, physical common sense, tracking objects, reading social cues. None of that feels like effort to us, but it's actually enormously complex, and it's not well represented in text. Meanwhile, the things we find hard, like competition math or writing a parser, are things we've written down a lot about, step by step, because we had to externalize our thinking to do them at all. So the training distribution is almost inverted relative to human difficulty. The models get a huge amount of signal on exactly the stuff we consider impressive, and comparatively little on the stuff we consider obvious.

The other piece is how the models actually process things. Tokenization is a good example. When a model fails at character counting, it's not that it's dumb, it's that it literally doesn't see letters the way you do. It's a bit like asking a person to count the pixels in a word. The failure tells you about the interface, not about the underlying capability. And a lot of the jaggedness is like that. It's artifacts of the representation, the training objective, the lack of grounding, rather than some deep deficit.

What I've found encouraging is that the frontier is jagged but it's also moving. Every time we identify one of these embarrassing gaps, it tends to close pretty quickly once there's a reason to target it. Reasoning models closed a lot of the gaps around multi-step arithmetic and planning that people assumed were fundamental. So I try not to read too much into any one failure. The question I ask is whether the failure is about a capability the model fundamentally lacks, or about a capability that just hasn't been elicited yet. And usually it's the latter.

The practical implication is that you have to actually test things on your own distribution. You can't look at a benchmark and extrapolate. The surface is weird enough that the only reliable way to know where the frontier is for your use case is to go poke at it.

r001.rationale: The response explains uneven capability through training data, tokenization, representation, and grounding, but does not attribute it to limited context.

r002.rationale: It discusses capabilities improving when targeted, but does not compare how naturally humans versus current AI models transfer lessons from one task to future tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the surprising thing is that difficulty for a model doesn’t line up neatly with difficulty for a human. You can have a model solve a really challenging math problem and then miss something that seems obvious in an everyday interaction. So it’s hard to put these systems on a single scale and say, “It’s this smart, therefore it should be able to do all these other things.”

Part of that is that they learn differently from us. Humans bring a lot of experience with the physical world and a lot of implicit context to a task. A model might have very strong capabilities in an area where it’s had useful training signals, but those capabilities don’t necessarily transfer in the way you’d expect.

That makes understanding the boundary really important. When you see an impressive result, you want to ask how reliably the model can do it, what happens when you change the setup, and whether it recognizes when it’s out of its depth. Smoothing out those inconsistencies is a big part of making the systems useful.

r001.rationale: The response links uneven capabilities to how models learn and contrasts their training signals with humans’ physical-world experience and implicit context.

r002.rationale: It contrasts human experience with models’ capabilities, which “don’t necessarily transfer” as expected, communicating that transfer is less natural for current models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the surprising thing is that capabilities don’t arrive in the order we expect. We tend to imagine intelligence as a ladder: first you master the easy things, then you move on to the hard things. But a model can solve a difficult math problem and then stumble on something that feels obvious to a person.

Part of that is that “easy” reflects our own experience. We’ve spent our whole lives interacting with the physical world and understanding social context. Models have a very different kind of experience, so their strengths and weaknesses don’t line up with ours.

That makes evaluation really important. Seeing a model do something impressive doesn’t mean you can assume it will handle everything that seems simpler. You have to understand where it’s reliable, where it needs help, and whether it can recognize when it’s out of its depth.

r001.rationale: The response links uneven capabilities to models having different experiences from people, but does not attribute them to limited context.

r002.rationale: It discusses differences in strengths and reliability, but does not compare how naturally humans and current AI models transfer lessons between tasks.
